description: REQ-106's critical section (lock acquire -> compute -> disburse -> ledger append -> lock release) and its own PROP-106f only specify fail-closed behavior for the case where payViaFacilitator ITSELF FAILS (facilitator unreachable, verify/settle rejects, tx reverts). Neither REQ-106's Edge Cases nor its Acceptance Criteria, nor PROP-106f, ever address the case where payViaFacilitator SUCCEEDS (a real on-chain transfer lands) but the holding process then crashes BEFORE ledger.js::appendChild(LOANS_LEDGER_PATH, row) durably writes the new loans.jsonl row. REQ-106's own Edge Cases list only says: 'The instance holding the lock crashes mid-issuance: the existing heartbeat + isLockStale mechanism reclaims the lock after staleMs of no heartbeat, exactly as it already does for gig-board operations -- REQ-106 does not need a second staleness mechanism.' This addresses ONLY the lock-reclaim mechanics, not the deeper consequence: because nextLoanSequenceForLender(loanRows, lenderId) is computed by reading the CURRENT ledger state (which still shows the crashed attempt's disbursement as never having happened, since its row was never appended), a SECOND caller that reclaims the stale lock will recompute the SAME sequence number `n` the crashed attempt had already computed and disbursed against -- and, if REQ-101/102's conditions still independently hold (which they likely do, since the crashed transfer left no trace in loans.jsonl to change the lender's outstandingPrincipalUsd or the borrower's outstanding-obligation status), will issue a SECOND real, independent on-chain transfer. The result is a genuine double-disbursement: real money leaves the lender's wallet twice, but loans.jsonl (append-only, one row per successful attempt) only ever records ONE of the two transfers as ever having happened -- the crashed attempt's real, on-chain, irreversible transfer becomes permanently untracked, unattributed to any loan_id, and unrepayable-against by design (nothing in loans.jsonl references it). Re-read this session, /Users/anicca/anicca/skills/economy/gig/lib/lock.mjs's own header comment documents that THIS EXACT LOCK MODULE was originally created to fix a real double-pay drain, but that historical bug was TWO CONCURRENT LOCKLESS callers racing past each other -- a scenario the lock genuinely closes. The lock provides no protection at all against a SINGLE holder's own crash occurring strictly between an external, irreversible side effect (the on-chain settle) and the local, durable bookkeeping write that is supposed to represent it -- exactly the vulnerability window this spec's own critical-section design (disbursement THEN append, inside one lock) creates and never closes.

evidence.snippet: Disbursement failure (resolves this revision's own FIND-003 ...): ... IF that call fails for ANY reason ... THE SYSTEM SHALL fail closed ... The instance holding the lock crashes mid-issuance: the existing heartbeat + isLockStale mechanism reclaims the lock after staleMs of no heartbeat ... REQ-106 does not need a second staleness mechanism.

crossCheck.note: The module's own header comment documents its motivating bug as two CONCURRENT lockless callers both reaching a real settle -- a scenario the lock structurally closes via exclusive file creation. It documents no protection for a single holder's own process crash occurring strictly between an already-succeeded external side effect (payViaFacilitator's on-chain settle) and the local ledger.js append meant to record it; isLockStale/reclaimStaleLock (lines 84-151) only reclaim the LOCK, they do not, and cannot, recover or detect an already-executed but unrecorded prior transfer.
